title: Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
subtitle: Official NTA/UGC Answer Key Attached (98/100 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the works of Thomas Carlyle in the chronological order of publication :
(A) Periods of European Culture
(B) Specimens of German Romance
(C) Heroes and Hero Worship
(D) German Literature
(E) Revolution of Modern Europe
items.explanation: The chronological order of Thomas Carlyle's works is Specimens of German Romance (1827), German Literature (1827 essays), Periods of European Culture (1838 lectures), Revolutions of Modern Europe (1839 lectures), and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841).

items.title: Q2 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Tughlag
(B) The Goddess Speaks
(C) My Forest
(D) Towards Marriage
(I) V. K Gokak
(II) M. V. Rama Sarma
(Ill) Girish Karnad
(IV) V. D. Trivedi
items.explanation: Girish Karnad wrote the historical play Tughlaq (1964, A-III); V. K. Gokak authored The Goddess Speaks (1948, B-I); V. D. Trivedi wrote My Forest (1949, C-IV); and M. V. Rama Sarma wrote the play Towards Marriage (1954, D-II).

items.title: Q3 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Stephen Dedalus appears as a character in :
(A) A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
(B) Mrs. Dalloway
(C) The Voyage Out
(D) Ulysses
(E) To the Light House
items.explanation: Stephen Dedalus is James Joyce's semi-autobiographical protagonist in A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) and a central character in Ulysses (1922). The other listed novels—Mrs. Dalloway, The Voyage Out, and To the Lighthouse—were written by Virginia Woolf.

items.title: Q4 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Which of the following poems are not by Robert Frost ?
(A) “An Old Man’s Winter Night”
(B) “The Grindstone”
(C) “The Smile”
(D) “Under the Balcony”
(E) “The New Remorse”
items.explanation: 'Under the Balcony' (1881) and 'The New Remorse' (1887) are poems composed by Oscar Wilde, not Robert Frost. In contrast, 'An Old Man's Winter Night' (1916), 'The Grindstone' (1923), and 'The Smile' are celebrated poems by Robert Frost.

items.title: Q5 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) The Wind Flower
(B) Enchantment and Sorrow
(C) Tin Flute
(D) Garden in the Wind
I. 1970
II. 1947
III. 1975
IV. 1984
items.explanation: French-Canadian author Gabrielle Roy published The Wind Flower in 1970 (A-I), her autobiography Enchantment and Sorrow in 1984 (B-IV), the English translation of The Tin Flute in 1947 (C-II), and Garden in the Wind in 1975 (D-III).

items.title: Q6 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Which of the following is not known as a ‘War Poet’ in English Literature ?
items.explanation: Rupert Brooke, Siegfried Sassoon, and Wilfred Owen are celebrated British First World War poets renowned for their frontline verse. John Maxfield is not a recognized war poet in English literature.

items.title: Q7 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: Who is the author of A Course in General Linguistics?
items.explanation: Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure authored Course in General Linguistics (Cours de linguistique générale), compiled from his lectures and published posthumously in 1916 by his students. The book established structural linguistics through fundamental distinctions such as signifier and signified, and langue and parole.

items.title: Q8 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following is not among the University Wits ?
items.explanation: Thomas Norton co-authored the first English blank-verse tragedy Gorboduc (1561) with Thomas Sackville, but he was a lawyer and politician rather than a dramatist among the University Wits. The University Wits were university-trained Elizabethan playwrights such as John Lyly, Thomas Nashe, George Peele, Robert Greene, and Christopher Marlowe.

items.title: Q9 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Studies in the History of the Renaissance by Walter Pater
(B) The French Revolution by Thomas Carlyle
(C) Unto this Last by John Ruskin
(D) The Making of England by John Richard Green
(E) On the Origin of Species by Charles Robert Darwin
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication is Thomas Carlyle's The French Revolution (1837), Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859), John Ruskin's Unto This Last (1860 in Cornhill / 1862), Walter Pater's Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873), and John Richard Green's The Making of England (1881).

items.title: Q10 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) The New India
(B) This Matter of Culture
(C) East of Home
(D) Light Luggage
(I) J. Krishnamurti
(II) Ved Mehta
(III) V. V. John
(IV) Santha Rama Rau
items.explanation: Ved Mehta authored The New India (1978, A-II); J. Krishnamurti wrote This Matter of Culture (1964, B-I); Santha Rama Rau wrote the Asian travelogue East of Home (1950, C-IV); and V. V. John published the essay collection Light Luggage (1969, D-III).

items.title: Q11 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Black Feminism pays attention to :
(A) The material lives of Black women
(B) The patriarchal nature of black society and traditions
(C) The growth of individualism
(D) The possibilities of ‘Sisterhood’ of black women
(E) Conforming to hetero sexual relationship only
items.explanation: Black Feminism centers on the material conditions of Black women (A), critiques patriarchal structures within Black communities (B), and builds collective sisterhood (D). Statements C and E are incorrect because Black Feminism rejects individualist detachment in favor of collective struggle, and it embraces queer and lesbian sexualities rather than conforming solely to heterosexuality.

items.title: Q12 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Lycidas is an example of which of the following?
items.explanation: John Milton's 'Lycidas' (1637) is a pastoral elegy written to mourn the death of his Cambridge classmate Edward King. It employs pastoral conventions by portraying both the speaker and King as shepherds tending their flocks while contemplating loss and mortality.

items.title: Q13 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Which of the following can be classified as Science Fiction ?
(A) The Moonlight
(B) Time Machine
(C) Great Expectations
(D) The Golden Gate
(E) Brave New World
items.explanation: H. G. Wells's The Time Machine (1895) and Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) are landmark works of science fiction dealing with time travel and totalitarian future biotechnology. Great Expectations is Victorian realist fiction, and The Golden Gate is a verse novel.

items.title: Q14 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Feminist literary and cultural theory draws a link between :
(A) The representation of women in art
(B) Examining how the privileging of some meanings is at the cost of others
(C) The real, material conditions in which women live
(D) The ideological basis of acts of imagination
(E) Providing the native with the means of resistance
items.explanation: Feminist literary and cultural theory explores how patriarchal ideologies depict women in art (A) and links these depictions directly to the historical, material conditions shaping women's real lives (C). The other statements describe poststructuralist textual critique or anti-colonial native resistance.

items.title: Q15 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Hymns in Darkness
(B) The Unfinished Man
(C) A Time to Change and Other Poems
(D) Sixty Poems
(E) The Exact Name
items.explanation: The chronological order of Nissim Ezekiel's poetry collections is A Time to Change (1952), Sixty Poems (1953), The Unfinished Man (1960), The Exact Name (1965), and Hymns in Darkness (1976).

items.title: Q16 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following is not correct about “Cognitive approach to language learning” ?
options: It lays emphasis on conscious acquisition of language
It seeks intellectual understanding by the learner
It seeks a reasonable understanding of structure of the language to develop better use of language
It rejects the teaching of grammar and language rules
items.explanation: The cognitive approach to language acquisition emphasizes conscious mental understanding and internalizing structural rules and grammar. Saying that it rejects the teaching of grammar and language rules is false, as explicit understanding of language structure is central to the cognitive model.

items.title: Q17 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Which of the following poets describes himself as “not an Indian poet but a poet writing a universal language of poetry, of feeling, of love and hate and sex”.
items.explanation: Modern Indian poet Arvind Krishna Mehrotra famously described himself as 'not an Indian poet but a poet writing a universal language of poetry, of feeling, of love and hate and sex'. He articulated this position to reject parochial nationalistic boundaries in poetic expression.

items.title: Q18 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) are true about “Synecdoche” ?
(A) It is a comparison between two objects
(B) It is a figure of speech in which part refers to the whole
(C) It is a figure of speech in which the name of an attribute is substituted for that of the thing meant
(D) It is a comparison between two unrelated objects
(E) It is a figure of speech in which the whole refers to a part
items.explanation: Synecdoche is a figure of speech in which a part refers to the whole (B), such as 'new wheels' for a car, or the whole refers to a part (E), such as 'society' for high society. Statement C describes metonymy, while A and D refer to similes or metaphors.

items.title: Q19 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who has written The Metaphysical Poets ?
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot published his landmark critical essay 'The Metaphysical Poets' in 1921 as a review of Herbert Grierson's anthology. In this essay, Eliot formulated the influential concepts of 'dissociation of sensibility' and the metaphysical capacity to feel thought as immediately as the odor of a rose.

items.title: Q20 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following is not an Empiricist Philosopher ?
items.explanation: René Descartes was a 17th-century Continental Rationalist who argued that knowledge is founded on reason and innate ideas ('Cogito, ergo sum'). Francis Bacon, John Locke, and David Hume are the leading British Empiricists who maintained that knowledge originates from sensory experience.

items.title: Q21 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following writers do not exclusively belong to the eighteenth century ?
(A) Oliver Goldsmith
(B) Thomas Gray
(C) Robert Southey
(D) William Cowper
(E) Charles Lamb
items.explanation: Robert Southey (1774–1843) and Charles Lamb (1775–1834) are key British Romantic authors whose major literary works appeared in the 19th century. Oliver Goldsmith, Thomas Gray, and William Cowper died in or before 1800 and belong exclusively to the eighteenth century.

items.title: Q22 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following is true about Aime Cesaire ?
(A) Aime Cesaire in best known for the term ‘negritude’
(B) Aime Cesaire was influenced by Harlem Renaissance
(C) Aime Cesaire wrote Wretched of the Earth
(D) Aime Cesaire was a feminist writer
(E) Aime Cesaire argued that colonialism was never a benevolent enterprise
items.explanation: Aimé Césaire co-founded the Négritude movement (A), drew significant inspiration from the Harlem Renaissance (B), and argued forcefully in Discourse on Colonialism that colonial enterprise was never benevolent (E). Statement C is false because The Wretched of the Earth was written by Frantz Fanon, and D is false because Césaire's primary theoretical focus was anti-colonialism and Black cultural identity rather than feminism.

items.title: Q23 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Metonymy
(B) Paradox
(C) Personification
(D) Metaphor
(I) Tell me not, Sweet, I am unkind
(II) Busy old fool, unruly Sun
(II) I enjoy reading Shakespeare
(IV) The river snakes its way through the mountains
items.explanation: Using 'Shakespeare' to mean his plays is Metonymy (A-III); Richard Lovelace's 'Tell me not, Sweet, I am unkind' introduces Paradox through the idea of leaving love for honor (B-I); John Donne's 'Busy old fool, unruly Sun' uses Personification (C-II); and describing a river as 'snaking' uses Metaphor (D-IV).

items.title: Q24 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
What is the correct chronological order of the following poets ?
(A) Thomas Carew
(B) Edward Herbert
(C) John Donne
(D) George Herbert
(E) James Shirley
items.explanation: The chronological order of these early modern poets by birth is John Donne (1572–1631), Edward Herbert, Lord Herbert of Cherbury (1583–1648), George Herbert (1593–1633), Thomas Carew (1595–1640), and James Shirley (1596–1666).

items.title: Q25 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following statements help in understanding the concept of ‘interdisciplinarity” ?
(A) Application of education beyond University
(B) Combination of two or more topics, disciplines or subject matters
(C) Focusing on one domain for one lesson
(D) The idea of bringing together diverse disciplines
(E) Education is for the people and their development at large
items.explanation: Interdisciplinarity involves crossing traditional disciplinary boundaries to apply education beyond conventional university departments (A) and synthesizing insights from diverse fields of study (D).

items.title: Q26 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Who among the following are not part of the Black Aesthetic Movement ?
(A) David Pepper
(B) Stuart Hall
(C) Alan Sinfield
(D) Anthony Appaiah
(E) Hazel Carby
items.explanation: David Pepper is an environmental geographer known for eco-socialist theory, and Alan Sinfield is a British Cultural Materialist and queer theorist, so neither was part of the Black Aesthetic Movement. Stuart Hall, Anthony Appiah, and Hazel Carby are prominent figures in Black and postcolonial cultural studies.

items.title: Q27 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: The line “That is no country for old men” figures in which of the following poems?
options: The Death of the Hired Man
items.explanation: 'That is no country for old men' is the famous opening line of W. B. Yeats's modernist poem 'Sailing to Byzantium', published in The Tower (1928). The line expresses the aging poet's sense of alienation from the sensual, fertile world of youth.

items.title: Q28 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Joseph Conrad in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Heart of Darkness
(B) Typhoon
(C) Under Western Eyes
(D) The Nigger of the Narcissus
(E) Outcast of the Islands
items.explanation: The chronological order of Joseph Conrad's works is An Outcast of the Islands (1896), The Nigger of the 'Narcissus' (1897), Heart of Darkness (1899 serial / 1902 book), Typhoon (1902 serial / 1903 book), and Under Western Eyes (1911).

items.title: Q29 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Christopher Marlowe
(B) William Shakespeare
(C) Thomas Kyd
(D) Ben Jonson
(I) The Winter’s Tale
(II) The Jew of Malta
(III) Every Man in his Humour
(IV) Spanish Tragedy
items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe wrote The Jew of Malta (c. 1589–1590, A-II); William Shakespeare wrote The Winter's Tale (c. 1611, B-I); Thomas Kyd wrote The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587–1590, C-IV); and Ben Jonson wrote Every Man in His Humour (1598, D-III).

items.title: Q30 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Choose the correct sequence for writing a research paper :
(A) Gathering Data
(B) Finding a Topic
(C) Finding and Reading the Best Sources
(D) Organizing Ideas and Setting Goals
(E) Writing the Paper
items.explanation: The standard sequence for preparing a research paper begins with finding a topic (B), gathering preliminary data (A), organizing ideas and setting goals (D), finding and reading the best sources (C), and finally writing the paper (E).

items.title: Q31 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The line “Drop drop, slow tears” is the example of :
items.explanation: 'Drop drop, slow tears' from Phineas Fletcher's hymn 'A Litany' contains consecutive heavily accented syllables. A metrical foot composed of two stressed syllables is a spondee.

items.title: Q32 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Trochee
(B) Dactyl
(C) Spondee
(D) Iambics
(I) Two stressed syllables
(II) One stressed followed by two unstressed syllables
(III) Stressed syllable followed by unstressed
(IV) Unstressed followed by stressed syllable
items.explanation: A trochee consists of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable (A-III); a dactyl consists of a stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables (B-II); a spondee consists of two stressed syllables (C-I); and an iamb consists of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable (D-IV).

items.title: Q33 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) “Preface to Fables, Ancient and Modern”
(B) “The Pleasures of Imagination”
(C) “The Function of Criticism”
(D) “The Imagination”
(I) Joseph Addison
(II) I. A. Richards
(IIl) John Dryden
(IV) TS. Eliot
items.explanation: John Dryden wrote the 'Preface to Fables, Ancient and Modern' (1700, A-III); Joseph Addison authored the series 'The Pleasures of the Imagination' in The Spectator (1712, B-I); T. S. Eliot published the critical essay 'The Function of Criticism' (1923, C-IV); and I. A. Richards examined 'The Imagination' in Principles of Literary Criticism (1924, D-II).

items.title: Q34 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Women’s Studies is focused and built upon :
(A) Feminist critique of knowledge
(B) Cultural response of the native
(C) Political nature of the critical race theory
(D) The shift from liberal feminist views to more socialist and radical views of gender roles and culture
(E) Production of texts only
items.explanation: Women's Studies developed from a systematic feminist critique of traditional academic knowledge (A), accompanied by a theoretical shift from early liberal feminism toward socialist and radical perspectives on gender and power (D).

items.title: Q35 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary texts in the order of their publication :
(A) The Dunciad
(B) Essay on Man
(C) The Rape of the Lock
(D) Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot
(E) Windsor Forest
items.explanation: The chronological order of Alexander Pope's works is The Rape of the Lock (1712), Windsor Forest (1713), The Dunciad (1728), An Essay on Man (1733–1734), and Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot (1735).

items.title: Q36 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary magazines in the chronological order of their origin or first appearance.
(A) The Westminster Review
(B) The Edinburgh Review
(C) The Quarterly Review
(D) Blackwood’s Magazine
(E) The London Magazine
items.explanation: The chronological order of these British periodicals by founding date is The Edinburgh Review (1802), The Quarterly Review (1809), Blackwood's Magazine (1817), The London Magazine (1820), and The Westminster Review (1824).

items.title: Q37 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who is the author of the French Revolution?
items.explanation: Thomas Carlyle wrote The French Revolution: A History, a three-volume masterwork published in 1837. The work is famous for its dramatic prose style and its depiction of historical events through the lens of moral retribution.

items.title: Q38 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Who wrote the famous book History of Dramatic English Literature?
items.explanation: Sir Adolphus William Ward (A. W. Ward) authored A History of English Dramatic Literature to the Death of Queen Anne, published in 1875. It is an authoritative historical survey of English drama from medieval liturgical plays through the Renaissance and Restoration.

items.title: Q39 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: The plays which are based on the Biblical stories are known as :
items.explanation: Mystery plays were medieval vernacular dramas based on Biblical narratives, depicting sacred events from the Creation to Doomsday. In contrast, Miracle plays dramatized the lives and miracles of saints, while Morality plays allegorized moral struggles between virtue and vice.

items.title: Q40 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Jane Eyre
(B) Henry Esmond
(C) The Lady of the Last Minstrel
(D) Mary Barton
(E) Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication is Walter Scott's narrative poem The Lay of the Last Minstrel (1805), Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre (1847), Elizabeth Gaskell's Mary Barton (1848), William Makepeace Thackeray's Henry Esmond (1852), and Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886).

items.title: Q41 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Archetypal Patterns in Poetry
(B) The Dynamics of Literary Response
(C) The Anxiety of Influence
(D) A Literature of their Own
(I) Norman Holland
(II) Harold Bloom
(IlI) Maud Bodkin
(IV) Elaine Showalter
items.explanation: Maud Bodkin published Archetypal Patterns in Poetry (1934, A-III); Norman Holland wrote The Dynamics of Literary Response (1968, B-I) applying psychoanalysis to reader response; Harold Bloom formulated The Anxiety of Influence (1973, C-II); and Elaine Showalter published A Literature of Their Own (1977, D-IV).

items.title: Q42 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are true about ‘cyberfeminism’?
(A) Women are not demanding material and social space
(B) Itinterrogates the patriarchal nature of the new Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
(C) It is a negotiation with the contemporary culture’s extensive informatization
(D) Virtual environment does not provide greater freedom to women
(E) Women are unable to appropriate the maternality of cyberspace
items.explanation: Cyberfeminism interrogates how patriarchal structures operate within information and communication technologies (B) and critically negotiates contemporary society's pervasive informatization (C). Statements A, D, and E are incorrect because cyberfeminists actively claim online spaces and view virtual environments as liberating for women.

items.title: Q43 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: Midnight’s Children is a representative text of :
items.explanation: Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981) is a representative text of postmodernism and historiographic metafiction. It uses magic realism, an unreliable narrator, and fragmented chronology to retell the story of modern India through the life of Saleem Sinai.

items.title: Q44 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Which of the following poems are by Sir Walter Scott ?
(A) “Christmas in the Olden Time”
(B) “After the Last Breath”
(C) “Lochinvar”
(D) “Dance of Death”
(E) “A Man was Drawing near to Me”
items.explanation: Sir Walter Scott wrote 'Christmas in the Olden Time' (Marmion, 1808, A), 'Lochinvar' (Marmion, C), and 'The Dance of Death' (1815, D). 'After the Last Breath' and 'A Man was Drawing near to Me' are poems composed by Thomas Hardy.

items.title: Q45 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Who is the author of French novel, Le Journal de Mademoiselle d’Arvers ?
items.explanation: Toru Dutt wrote Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers, published posthumously in Paris in 1879. It was the first novel in the French language written by an Indian author.

items.title: Q46 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who has written Jejuri?
items.explanation: Arun Kolatkar wrote Jejuri (1976), a poetic cycle of thirty-one poems depicting a modern skeptic's journey to the temple town of Khandoba in Maharashtra. The book was awarded the Commonwealth Poetry Prize in 1977.

items.title: Q47 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Postmodernism
(B) Psychoanalysis
(C) Mimicry
(D) New Historicism
(I) Jacques Lacan
(II) Stephen Greenblatt
(III) Jean Baudrillard
(IV) Homi Bhabha
items.explanation: Jean Baudrillard is a leading theorist of Postmodernism and hyperreality (A-III); Jacques Lacan reformulated Psychoanalysis using linguistic structures (B-I); Homi Bhabha theorized postcolonial Mimicry in The Location of Culture (C-IV); and Stephen Greenblatt pioneered New Historicism (D-II).

items.title: Q48 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who is the author of Abhijanasakuntalam?
items.explanation: Classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist Kalidasa authored the renowned drama Abhijnanasakuntalam (The Recognition of Shakuntala). The play dramatizes the epic love story of King Dushyanta and Shakuntala.

items.title: Q49 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Untouchable
(B) Serpent and the Rope
(C) Nectar in a Sieve
(D) A Tiger for Malgudi
(I) Raja Rao
(II) R. K. Narayan
(II) Mulk Raj Anand
(IV) Kamala Markandeya
items.explanation: Mulk Raj Anand wrote Untouchable (1935, A-III); Raja Rao authored The Serpent and the Rope (1960, B-I); Kamala Markandaya published Nectar in a Sieve (1954, C-IV); and R. K. Narayan wrote A Tiger for Malgudi (1983, D-II).

items.title: Q50 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: Of the following, what is not true about Pidgins and Creoles ?
options: Spoken by the Third World Countries
New languages in their own right
Developed during the periods of linguistic crisis
items.explanation: Linguists reject the claim that pidgins and creoles are 'distorted versions of other languages'; they are systematic, fully functional languages with their own stable grammatical rules. They typically develop in multilingual contact situations during periods of trade, migration, or linguistic crisis.

items.title: Q51 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: “The Frontiers of Criticism” by T.S. Eliot is associated with :
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot delivered 'The Frontiers of Criticism' in 1956 at the University of Minnesota, directly addressing the scope and limits of New Criticism. In the essay, Eliot famously cautioned against the excessive textual dissection of the 'lemon-squeezer' school of criticism.

items.title: Q52 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following poets are called ‘Graveyard poets’?
(A) W.B. Yeats
(B) Thomas Parnell
(C) Edward Young
(D) T.S. Eliot
(E) Robert Blair
items.explanation: Thomas Parnell ('Night-Piece on Death', 1721), Edward Young (Night-Thoughts, 1742–1745), and Robert Blair (The Grave, 1743) are known as the Graveyard Poets for their melancholic verse on death and mortality. W. B. Yeats and T. S. Eliot are 20th-century modernists.

items.title: Q53 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In Patrick White’s Voss, the character Voss is :
options: a crazy German trying to make his experience worthwhile
items.explanation: In Patrick White's Voss (1957), Johann Ulrich Voss's outward trek across the Australian desert is primarily an inward, metaphysical journey of exploring his self and wrestling with spiritual pride and mortality.

items.title: Q54 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Robert Browning’s “My Last Duchess” is an example of :
items.explanation: Robert Browning's 'My Last Duchess' (1842) is a classic dramatic monologue. Through a single continuous speech to an envoy, the Duke of Ferrara unwittingly reveals his jealousy, controlling arrogance, and moral corruption.

items.title: Q55 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which of the following was not an Irish playwright ?
items.explanation: Harold Pinter was an English playwright born in Hackney, London, who won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Literature. George Bernard Shaw, J. M. Synge, and Oscar Wilde were all born in Ireland and belong to the Irish dramatic tradition.

items.title: Q56 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their appearance in the English Literary Scene :
(A) Art for Art’s sake
(B) Epistolary Novel
(C) Metaphysical Poetry
(D) Epic Theatre
(E) Stream of Consciousness Technique
items.explanation: The chronological order of appearance in English literary history is Metaphysical Poetry (early 17th century), the Epistolary Novel (mid-18th century), Art for Art's sake (late 19th century Aestheticism), the Stream of Consciousness Technique (early 20th-century modernism), and Epic Theatre (Bertolt Brecht, 1920s–1930s).

items.title: Q57 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following is considered as the first published composition in English by an Indian ?
items.explanation: Caveli Venkata Boriah's 'Accounts of the Jains', published in 1807 in the journal Asiatic Researches, is historically recognized as the first published English composition written by an Indian.

items.title: Q58 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Afro-American Literature
(B) Caribbean literature
(C) Australian Aboriginal literature
(D) Dalit Literature
(I) Basudev Sunani
(I) Sally Morgan
(Ill) V. S. Naipaul
(IV) Zora Neale Hurston
items.explanation: Zora Neale Hurston is an African American writer of the Harlem Renaissance (A-IV); V. S. Naipaul is an acclaimed Caribbean author (B-III); Sally Morgan is an Australian Aboriginal writer known for My Place (C-II); and Basudev Sunani is a prominent Odia Dalit poet and author (D-I).

items.title: Q59 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who wrote the famous text Dignity of Man ?
items.explanation: Thomas More translated Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's Life of John Picus Earl of Mirandula into English around 1505, introducing Renaissance humanist ideas regarding human dignity into English literature. More's humanist writings, including Utopia, consistently defend human dignity and reason.

items.title: Q60 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publications :
(A) Love and Death
(B) Urvasie : A Poem
(C) Songs to Myrtilla
(D) Savitri
(E) Chitrangada
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication is Sri Aurobindo's Songs to Myrtilla (1895), Sri Aurobindo's Urvasie (1896), Rabindranath Tagore's Chitrangada (published in English in 1914 / written 1892), Sri Aurobindo's Love and Death (written 1899, published 1921), and Sri Aurobindo's epic Savitri (1950).

items.title: Q61 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: The line “Because I could not stop for Death-He kindly stopped for me” figures in whose poetry ?
items.explanation: 'Because I could not stop for Death— / He kindly stopped for me' is the opening quatrain of Emily Dickinson's Poem 479, written around 1863. The poem personifies Death as a polite, courteous carriage driver accompanying the speaker toward eternity.

items.title: Q62 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publications :
(A) Hemachandra Joshi’s Plays for the Young
(B) Balwant Gargi’s The Knife
(C) P. K. Bosu’s Conrad and Leonora
(D) Abdul Mi’s The Land of Twilight
(E) D. M. Borgaonkar’s Image Breakers
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication of these Indian English plays is P. K. Bosu's Conrad and Leonora (1888), Hemachandra Joshi's Plays for the Young (early 20th century), Abdul Ali's The Land of Twilight (1937), D. M. Borgaonkar's Image Breakers (1938), and Balwant Gargi's The Knife (1971).

items.title: Q63 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Who made this following statement ?
“Truly neither philosopher nor historiographer could have entered into the gates of popular judgments, if they had not taken a great passport of poetry”.
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney wrote this line in An Apology for Poetry (published 1595), arguing that poetry serves as the first light-giver to knowledge and that philosophers and historians historically entered popular consciousness through the engaging power of verse.

items.title: Q64 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following are correct about the components Romantic epistemology ?
(A) The active-projective view of human self or mind
(B) Mechanical, impersonal and artificial
(C) Distrust of reason
(D) Belief in reason
(E) Collectivism
items.explanation: Romantic epistemology is characterized by an active-projective view of the human mind as a creative source of perception (A) and a fundamental distrust of dry Enlightenment rationalism in favor of emotion and imagination (C).

items.title: Q65 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following periods in African American writing is called “Harlem Renaissance”?
items.explanation: The Harlem Renaissance emerged in New York in the late 1910s following the Great Migration, with 1917–1920 marking its vital formative period of African American literary and artistic expression.

items.title: Q66 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: Who introduced the concept of “Biopower” ?
items.explanation: French theorist Michel Foucault introduced the concept of 'biopower' (biopouvoir) in The History of Sexuality, Volume 1 (1976), referring to the regulatory and disciplinary practices used by modern states to control and manage human biological life.

items.title: Q67 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following is not connected to postmodernism?
(A) Self-reflexivity
(B) Industrialisation
(C) Magic Realism
(D) Absolutism
(E) Hybridity of Styles
items.explanation: Industrialisation is a defining feature of modernity and the industrial age rather than postmodernism's information economy (B), and Absolutism is fundamentally rejected by postmodernism's anti-foundationalism, relativism, and skepticism toward metanarratives (D).

items.title: Q68 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary texts in the order of their publication :
(A) The Taming of the Shrew
(B) Love’s Labour Lost
(C) The Merchant of Venice
(D) Much Ado About Nothing
(E) The Winter’s Tale
items.explanation: The chronological order of Shakespeare's plays by composition and performance is The Taming of the Shrew (c. 1590–1592), Love's Labour's Lost (c. 1594–1595), The Merchant of Venice (c. 1596–1597), Much Ado About Nothing (c. 1598–1599), and The Winter's Tale (c. 1610–1611).

items.title: Q69 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who wrote “A Defence of Hindoo Theism”?
items.explanation: Raja Ram Mohan Roy published 'A Defence of Hindoo Theism' in 1817 to defend Upanishadic monotheism and rational religious reform against conservative critics.

items.title: Q70 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) A House of Mr. Biswas
(B) An Area of Darkness
(C) India: A Million Mutinies now
(D) A Bend in the River
I. 1979
II. 1961
III. 1964
IV. 1990
items.explanation: V. S. Naipaul published the novel A House for Mr. Biswas in 1961 (A-II), the travel narrative An Area of Darkness in 1964 (B-III), India: A Million Mutinies Now in 1990 (C-IV), and the novel A Bend in the River in 1979 (D-I).

items.title: Q71 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Which of the following books are not authored by Chinua Achebe ?
(A) Weep not Child
(B) A Grain of Wheat
(C) Things Fall Apart
(D) The Arrow of God
(E) The Petals of Blood
items.explanation: Weep Not, Child (1964), A Grain of Wheat (1967), and Petals of Blood (1977) are postcolonial novels written by Kenyan author Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, not Chinua Achebe. Achebe authored Things Fall Apart (1958) and Arrow of God (1964).

items.title: Q72 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In the poem “Dover Beach” Matthew Arnold speaks about :
(A) The sea which is calm literally and metaphorically
(B) The sea of faith which was once at its fullest
(C) The premonition experienced by Sophocles long ago
(D) The uselessness of love
(E) The war between England and France
items.explanation: In Matthew Arnold's 'Dover Beach' (1867), the speaker reflects on the literal and metaphorical calm of the sea (A), laments the retreat of the historical Sea of Faith (B), and recalls how Sophocles heard the same sad human condition on the Aegean (C).

items.title: Q73 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: “These English songs gravel one to death”. This statement is attributed to :
items.explanation: Scottish poet Robert Burns made this remark in his letters while collecting and preserving traditional Scottish songs, criticizing the artificiality of contemporary English songwriting compared to authentic folk lyrics.

items.title: Q74 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
The first English tragedy “Gorboduc” was written by :
(A) Nicholas Udall
(B) Thomas Sackville
(C) Thomas Norton
(D) Thomas Lyly
(E) John Heywood
items.explanation: Gorboduc (1561), the earliest English tragedy in blank verse, was co-authored by Thomas Sackville and Thomas Norton and performed before Queen Elizabeth I at the Inner Temple.

items.title: Q75 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary movements in the chronological order :
(A) Feminist Criticism
(B) Deconstruction
(C) Russian Formalism
(D) Phenomenological Criticism
(E) Cultural Studies
items.explanation: The chronological order of emergence for these literary movements is Russian Formalism (c. 1915), Phenomenological Criticism (1930s–1950s), Feminist Criticism (prominently late 1960s), Deconstruction (Jacques Derrida, 1966–1967), and Cultural Studies (consolidated in the 1970s and 1980s).

items.title: Q76 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who is the author of Mano Majra ?
items.explanation: Khushwant Singh wrote Mano Majra (1956), a renowned novel about the human tragedy of the 1947 Partition, which was later republished under the title Train to Pakistan.

items.title: Q77 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following was not a modernist writer ?
items.explanation: Henry Fielding was an 18th-century Augustan novelist and playwright known for works such as Joseph Andrews (1742) and Tom Jones (1749). James Joyce, Virginia Woolf, and D. H. Lawrence are seminal early 20th-century modernists.

items.title: Q78 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
John Osborne’s play Look Back in Anger
(A) Represented real confusions among real people of the 1950’s
(B) Is more important as a cultural phenomenon than as work of literature
(C) Is about a provincial graduate of humble social background
(D) Is about the upper-class society of 1990’s
(E) Is Victorian in its outlook
items.explanation: John Osborne's Look Back in Anger (1956) captured the authentic frustrations of post-war British society in the 1950s (A), became a defining cultural phenomenon launching the 'Angry Young Men' movement (B), and centered on working-class graduate Jimmy Porter (C).

items.title: Q79 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Nadine Gordimer is a :
items.explanation: Nadine Gordimer was a White South African novelist and essayist whose work vigorously challenged apartheid and racial injustice. She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991.

items.title: Q80 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following is not a Feminist Critic?
items.explanation: Emily Brontë was a 19th-century Victorian novelist and poet celebrated for Wuthering Heights (1847), not a feminist literary critic. Simone de Beauvoir, Judith Butler, and Virginia Woolf are major theorists in the history of feminist criticism.

items.title: Q81 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Sons and Lovers
(B) Waiting for Godot
(C) A Midsummer Night’s Dream
(D) A Room of One’s Own
(I) New Historicism
(II) Feminism
(IlI) Psychoanalysis
(IV) Postmodernism
items.explanation: D. H. Lawrence's Sons and Lovers deals with the Oedipus complex, making it a classic subject of Psychoanalytic criticism (A-III); Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot represents Postmodern and Absurdist theatre (B-IV); Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream is famously read through New Historicism (C-I); and Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own is a foundational text of Feminist theory (D-II).

items.title: Q82 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Gabriel Garcia Marquez is famous for which of the following ?
items.explanation: Colombian Nobel laureate Gabriel García Márquez is the preeminent master of Magic Realism, brilliantly weaving supernatural elements into realistic historical settings in novels such as One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967).

items.title: Q83 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) “So much depends upon a red wheel barrow”
(B) “Your mind and you are our Sargasso Sea”
(C) “Spring is like a perhaps hand (which comes carefully out of nowhere) arranging a window”
(D) “I caught the cold flash of the blue unappearable sky”
(I) Ezra Pound
(II) Stanley Kunitz
(III) William Carlos Williams
(IV) E. E. Cummings
items.explanation: William Carlos Williams wrote the Imagist poem 'The Red Wheelbarrow' containing 'So much depends upon a red wheel barrow' (A-III); Ezra Pound penned 'Portrait d'une Femme' opening with 'Your mind and you are our Sargasso Sea' (B-I); E. E. Cummings wrote 'Spring is like a perhaps hand' (C-IV); and Stanley Kunitz wrote 'I caught the cold flash of the blue unappearable sky' (D-II).

items.title: Q84 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) The moment of protagonist’s recognition in a narrative
(B) The decisive turn in tragedy by which the plot is resolved
(C) The inversion of an already established sequence
(D) The figure by which something distasteful is described in less repugnant terms
(I) Catastrophe
(II) Chiasmas
(IIl) Anagnorisis
(IV) Euphemism
items.explanation: In dramatic and literary terms, the protagonist's moment of recognition is Anagnorisis (A-III); the decisive resolving turn in tragedy is Catastrophe (B-I); the inverted sequence of terms (AB-BA) is Chiasmus (C-II); and substituting a mild expression for a harsh one is Euphemism (D-IV).

items.title: Q85 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Globalization is antithetical to :
(A) The movement of capital
(B) The movement of commodities
(C) Cultural nationalism
(D) People
(E) Narcissism
items.explanation: Globalization promotes transnational capital, goods, and cross-border migration, but it is antithetical to closed cultural nationalism (C) and insular narcissism (E) by fostering global interdependence and eroding parochial borders.

items.title: Q86 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Deductive method of research intends to :
items.explanation: The deductive research method moves from the general to the particular, beginning with a general theoretical framework or hypothesis and testing it against specific empirical observations. In contrast, inductive research moves from particular observations to general conclusions.

items.title: Q87 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: According to Edward Albert, the years 1550-1630 is known as :
items.explanation: In Edward Albert's History of English Literature, the period 1550–1630 is classified as 'The Age of Elizabeth', covering Elizabethan and early Jacobean poetry, drama, and prose.

items.title: Q88 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Animal Farm
(B) A Burnt Out Case
(C) The Mill on the Floss
(D) The Book of Snobs
(E) A Tale of Two Cities
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication is William Makepeace Thackeray's The Book of Snobs (1848), Charles Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities (1859), George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss (1860), George Orwell's Animal Farm (1945), and Graham Greene's A Burnt-Out Case (1960/1961).

items.title: Q89 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who defined criticism as “disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world” ?
items.explanation: Matthew Arnold famously defined criticism as a 'disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world' in his 1864 essay 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time'.

items.title: Q90 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Who has written The Myth of Sisyphus ?
items.explanation: Albert Camus wrote the philosophical essay The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), in which he articulated his philosophy of the Absurd through the mythological figure of Sisyphus endlessly pushing his boulder up the hill.

items.title: Q91 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Reading Comprehension · Reading Comprehension
items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Prose Passage]
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"They define virtue to be life ordered according to nature, and that we be made by God for that end; but that nature doth allure and provoke us to a joy of life, that is to say to pleasure, as to the end of all our operations. But they think that not in every pleasure, but only in that which is good and honest, the felicity of man consisteth. For to virtue, say they, our nature is led by happiness, as to the chief and highest good. But of all pleasures they reckon those to be the chief which are seated in the mind, whereof the contemplation of virtue and the consciousness of a good life are the greatest. For bodily pleasure they think is to be desired only for health's sake, and that pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure."
— Thomas More, Utopia (Book II)

Question:
What according to the Utopians, is the worse enemy of pleasure?
items.explanation: In Thomas More's Utopia (Book II), the passage explicitly declares that 'pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure', explaining why Utopians prize mental and moral virtues over fleeting bodily indulgences.

items.title: Q92 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Reading Comprehension · Reading Comprehension

For bodily pleasure they think is to be desired only for health's sake, and that pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure."
— Thomas More, Utopia (Book II)

Question:
Which of the following figures of speech could be appropriately read in the last sentence of the passage ?
items.explanation: The final sentence employs synecdoche by taking the specific bodily experience of 'pain' and the physical state of 'health' as representative parts standing for the overall condition of human physical suffering and well-being.

Question:
According to the Utopians, what is the nature of relation between health and pleasure ?
options: Health and pleasure are not related to each other
Health and pleasure are simply matters of imagination

Question:
What is the nature of prose used in the passage ?
items.explanation: The passage uses argumentative prose as More's narrator systematically defines virtue according to nature, constructs a rational case for why mental pleasures surpass bodily ones, and evaluates human conduct logically.

items.title: Q95 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Reading Comprehension · Reading Comprehension
items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Prose Passage]
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"They define virtue to be life ordered according to nature, and that we be made by God for that end; but that nature doth allure and provoke us to a joy of life, that is to say to pleasure, as to the end of all our operations. But they think that not in every pleasure, but only in that which is good and honest, the felicity of man consisteth. For to virtue, say they, our nature is led by happiness, as to the chief and highest good. But of all pleasures they reckon those to be the chief which are seated in the mind, whereof the contemplation of virtue and the consciousness of a good life are the greatest. For bodily pleasure they think is to be desired only for health's sake, and that pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure."
— Thomas More, Utopia (Book II)

Question:
What does the first line of the passage say about external stimulus ?
options: External stimulus is necessary condition for the experience of health
External stimulus is irrelevant to the experience of health
External stimulus is the by-product of health
items.explanation: The opening sentence explains that 'nature doth allure and provoke us to a joy of life', indicating that external natural stimuli and provocations are necessary conditions that lead and awaken humanity to the experience of health and pleasure.

items.title: Q96 · Sep 2024 (Re-conduct Shift 2)
items.meta: Reading Comprehension · Reading Comprehension
items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Poem]
Read the following poem carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Between my finger and my thumb
The squat pen rests; snug as a gun.
Under my window, a clean rasping sound
When the spade sinks into gravelly ground:
My father, digging. I look down
Till his straining rump among the flowerbeds
Bends low, comes up twenty years away
Stooping in rhythm through potato drills
Where he was digging.
The coarse boot nestled on the lug, the shaft
Against the inside knee was levered firmly.
He rooted out tall tops, buried the bright edge deep
To scatter new potatoes that we picked,
Loving their cool hardness in our hands.
By God, the old man could handle a spade.
Just like his old man.
My grandfather cut more turf in a day
Than any other man on Toner's bog.
Once I carried him milk in a bottle
Corked sloppily with paper. He straightened up
To drink it, then fell to right away
Nicking and slicing neatly, heaving sods
Over his shoulder, going down and down
For the good turf. Digging.
The cold smell of potato mould, the squelch and slap
Of soggy peat, the curt cuts of an edge
Through living roots awaken in my head.
But I've no spade to follow men like them.
Between my finger and my thumb
The squat pen rests.
I'll dig with it."
— Seamus Heaney, "Digging" 

Question:
The comparison of gun to a pen in the poem signifies :
options: the power of written word to bring about change
that the act of writing can be as lethal as using a weapon
the high administration of the speaker about father’s ability to use both pen and spade
items.explanation: In the opening stanza of Seamus Heaney's 'Digging', the simile comparing the pen to a gun ('snug as a gun') suggests that the writer's craft can wield decisive agency, deadly precision, and power comparable to a weapon.
